title: Angles on a line, round a point and opposite
keyIdea: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. Angles round a point add up to 360°. Where two straight lines cross, vertically opposite angles are equal, and angles next to each other add up to 180°. To find a missing angle, take the angles you know away from 180° or 360°, and name the fact you used, because diagrams are not drawn to scale.
familyTip: Cross two pencils on a table and ask which angles match and why. Then lay one pencil along a ruler and open the other like a door: point to the two angles on the ruler's edge and ask what they add up to, however wide the door opens. For a missing angle, ask “Which fact did you use?” as well as “What is it?”

visual.caption: Which fact fits? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: turn a ray on a line, find missing angles, share a full turn between three rays, match opposite angles, then give a reason for every angle.

kid: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. A straight line is a half turn. A ray can split it into two angles. When one gets bigger, the other gets smaller, but together they always make 180°. So if one is 130°, the other is 180° − 130° = 50°.

Angles round a point add up to 360°. That is a full turn. If three equal angles meet at a point, each one is 360° ÷ 3 = 120°. To find a missing angle, add the ones you know. Then take the total away from 360°.

When two straight lines cross, they make four angles. The angles opposite each other are equal. We call them vertically opposite angles. The angles next to each other sit on a straight line, so they add up to 180°.
Diagrams are often not drawn to scale. So do not guess an angle by how it looks. Find it with a fact, and say which fact you used: straight line, round a point, or vertically opposite.
adult: Ages 10 to 11. Year 6 of the National Curriculum in England asks pupils to recognise angles where they meet at a point, are on a straight line, or are vertically opposite, and to find missing angles. It builds on Year 5, where pupils learned that a straight line is 180° and a full turn is 360°. From 11 to 13 the same facts are used in longer chains with algebra.

Why the facts hold: a straight line is a half turn, so the angles along it fill 180°. A full turn is 360°. Where two lines cross, angles a and b sit on one line, so a + b = 180°. Angles b and c sit on the other line, so b + c = 180°. So a = c. This is Euclid's proof in Book I of the Elements.

Common mistakes: using 360° for a straight line, or 180° round a point; thinking the angles next to each other are equal; taking away from 90° instead of 180°; giving the total of the known angles as the answer; and reading an angle off the picture. Ask which fact your child used. They should name it, not just give a number.

In the lab your child turns a ray on a line and watches a + b stay at 180°, picks missing angles from chips that hide the usual slips, and turns three rays round a point until each angle is 120°. They also tap the partner of a yellow angle as two lines cross, and choose a reason card for each angle in a crossing.

practice.prompt: Two angles are on a straight line. One is 70°. What is the other?
practice.hint: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°, not 360° or 90°.
practice.explain: 180° − 70° = 110°. 290° used a full turn and 20° used a right angle.

practice.prompt: Two angles sit on a straight line. One is {a}°. What is the other, in degrees?
practice.hint: A straight line is a half turn: the two angles add up to 180°.
practice.explain: Angles on a straight line add to 180°, so the other is 180° − {a}° = {=180-a}°.

practice.prompt: Three angles meet round a point: {a}°, {b}° and x. What is x, in degrees?
practice.hint: Add the two angles you know, then take the total away from 360°.
practice.explain: Angles round a point add to 360°: 360° − {a}° − {b}° = {=360-a-b}°.

practice.prompt: Two straight lines cross. One angle is 64°. What is the angle opposite it?
practice.hint: Opposite angles at a crossing are a matching pair.
practice.explain: Vertically opposite angles are equal, so it is 64°. 116° is the angle next to it.

practice.prompt: Two straight lines cross. One angle is {a}°. What is the angle next to it, in degrees?
practice.hint: The angle next to it shares a straight line with it.
practice.explain: Angles next to each other at a crossing lie on a straight line: 180° − {a}° = {=180-a}°.

pool.prompt: What do the angles round a point add up to?
pool.hint: Going all the way round a point is one full turn.
pool.explain: A full turn is 360°, so the angles round a point add up to 360°. 180° is a straight line.

pool.prompt: Three angles on a straight line are {a}°, {b}° and x. What is x, in degrees?
pool.hint: Add the angles you know and take the total away from 180°.
pool.explain: Angles on a straight line add to 180°: 180° − {a}° − {b}° = {=180-a-b}°.

pool.prompt: Two straight lines cross. One angle is 125°. Which list shows all four angles in order round the point?
pool.hint: Opposite angles match; angles next to each other add to 180°.
pool.explain: Next to 125° is 180° − 125° = 55°, and opposite angles are equal: 125°, 55°, 125°, 55°. They add to 360°.

pool.prompt: Four angles meet round a point: {a}°, {b}°, {a}° and x. What is x, in degrees?
pool.hint: Add all three known angles, then take the total from 360°.

pool.prompt: Dan says the angle next to 40° on a straight line is 320°. What went wrong?
choices: He added instead of taking away
pool.hint: Work out 180° − 40° and compare it with Dan's answer.
pool.explain: 360° − 40° = 320°, so Dan used a full turn. On a straight line it is 180° − 40° = 140°.

pool.prompt: An angle in a diagram looks like a right angle, but there is no square mark. What should you do?
choices: Work it out with an angle fact
pool.hint: Are diagrams in questions always drawn to scale?
pool.explain: Diagrams are often not drawn to scale, and only a square mark shows a right angle. Use a fact to find it.

pool.prompt: {n} equal angles meet round a point. How big is each one, in degrees?
pool.hint: Share the full turn of 360° equally between the angles.

pool.prompt: Two straight lines cross. Angle a is 30°. Angle b is next to it, and angle c is opposite b. What is c?
pool.hint: Find b first with the straight-line fact, then use opposite angles.
pool.explain: b = 180° − 30° = 150° (straight line), and c is opposite b, so c = 150° too.

pool.prompt: Why are vertically opposite angles always equal?
choices: Each one makes 180° with the same angle between them
The lines are the same length
pool.hint: Look at the angle that sits next to both of them.
pool.explain: a + b = 180° and c + b = 180°, with the same b in both. So a and c must be equal.
